description: Cancer research generates huge amounts of data from many platforms, including next-generation sequencing and transcriptomics. To effectively analyze and interpret this data, researchers need to be equipped with specialized bioinformatics skills and a deep understanding of cancer genomics.  Through lectures and hands-on labs, this 5-day CBW course will provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles of genomic cancer analysis. Each lecture-lab module is designed as a distinct unit and all materials will be available open-access after the workshop concludes.
prerequisites: UNIX familiarity is required. You will also require your own laptop computer. Minimum requirements: 1024×768 screen resolution, 1.5GHz CPU, 2GB RAM, 10GB free disk space, recent versions of Windows, Mac OS X or Linux (Most computers purchased in the past 3-4 years likely meet these requirements). If you do not have access to your own computer, you may loan one from the CBW. Please contact support@bioinformatics.ca for more information. This workshop requires participants to complete pre-workshop tasks and readings.
title: (2026) Cancer Analysis: Toronto, ON

description:
From datasets and code to podcasts, reports, and performances, not all research outputs take the form of journal articles or books. These are known as Non-Traditional Research Outputs (NTROs): scholarly or creative works that fall outside conventional academic publishing. While NTROs make up a significant and growing part of research activity, they are often under-recognized in systems that track and assess research impact. In this workshop, participants will explore current best practices for tracking and communicating the impact of NTROs and learn how these practices align with movements such as the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), which advocates for more responsible and inclusive approaches to research assessment.

This workshop is part of the DORA (San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment) Workshop Series, which explores practical approaches for showcasing and evaluating research beyond traditional metrics. Together, these sessions focus on strengthening researcher visibility, communicating research impact, and recognizing the value of diverse scholarly contributions.

This session is ideal for researchers, creators, and academic staff working with non-traditional outputs who want to make their work more visible, trackable, and valued.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

1. Create persistent identifiers (e.g., DOIs) and metadata records for NTROs.
2. Incorporate NTROs into existing researcher profile systems (e.g., ORCID and McMaster Experts).
3. Identify strategies for increasing the visibility, discoverability, and impact of NTROs.
4. Communicate the value of NTROs within responsible research assessment frameworks.

**Details:** Any preparatory work for the session can be found on its [information page.](https://learn.scds.ca/ri26-27/ntros.html) This virtual workshop will be recorded and shared on the same page, and discoverable via the Sherman Centre's [Online Learning Catalogue.](https://scds.ca/searchable-online-learning/)

**Certificate Eligibility:** This workshop is eligible for the Sherman Centre's certificate program. For more information, visit [scds.ca/certificate-program](http://scds.ca/certificate-program). It is also eligible for the Canadian Certificate for Digital Humanities. To learn more, visit [ccdhhn.ca](http://ccdhhn.ca/) or contact [scds@mcmaster.ca](mailto:scds@mcmaster.ca).
organizer: The Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (SCDS)
title: DORA: Tracking the Impact of Non-Traditional Research Outputs

description:
Are you interested in sharing your educational materials for students and instructors to use and learn from? This workshop will focus on taking the content you’ve already created and turning it into an open educational resource (OER), without a lot of time or effort. We’ll discuss strategies for publishing and sharing educational content such as lecture notes, slide decks, assessments, or multimedia. We’ll find simple ways to openly share educational resources so that others can access, share, and adapt them. We’ll focus on expanding access to educational materials, with one small, ugly step at a time.

This session is ideal for instructors, teaching assistants, educational developers, librarians, and anyone interested in sharing educational materials more openly. No prior experience with OER creation or open licensing is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

1. Explain what is meant by “open educational resources”
2. Select an appropriate open license for a resource they might share
3. Identify online repositories where they might share an OER that they create

**Details:** Any preparatory work for the session can be found on its [information page](https://learn.scds.ca/dmds26-27/small-ugly.html). This virtual workshop will be recorded and shared on the same page, and discoverable via the Sherman Centre's [Online Learning Catalogue.](https://scds.ca/searchable-online-learning/)

description:
Every AI tool comes with a license agreement, and every license agreement is a privacy decision. The terms buried in that click determine where data gets processed, whether inputs train models, and what happens when something goes wrong. For researchers using AI for grant drafts, correspondence, and administrative work, the terms they accept is often the single biggest privacy risk factor and most never read it.

This session takes a practical, risk-based approach to AI adoption in research environments. It starts with what researchers are actually agreeing to when they sign up for AI tools breaking down terms of service patterns across free-tier, institutional, and enterprise licenses, and showing how the same tool can carry fundamentally different risk profiles depending on which version you're using. A paid personal ChatGPT account and an Bedrock API agreement have substantially different privacy implications.

The session then covers the inherent risks that follow from those agreements: data ingestion and retention, secondary use of inputs for model training, cross-border processing under foreign jurisdiction, hallucinated outputs, and the gap between marketing promises and contractual commitments. From there, attendees work through a practical decision matrix built for how research labs actually work. It weighs the sensitivity of the task drafting a grant versus handling ethics board data against what the tool's license actually allows: where processing happens, whether inputs are retained or used for training, and what commitments are contractual versus marketing. The result is a clear call for each use case: use with guardrails, or consider alternatives.

**About the Speaker**
Taylor Bohn is a Senior Privacy and Information Security Risk Advisor at the University of British Columbia (UBC), where he supports the evaluation and adoption of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, cloud services, and research platforms. His work centers on translating privacy, security, and governance requirements into practical decision-making guidance for institutional project teams. Taylor regularly conducts Privacy Impact Assessments, advises on AI governance, and presents on privacy, cybersecurity, and responsible technology adoption within higher education and the research community.
organizer: National Security Council (NSC) - Security Training and Awareness Group
title: Before You Click Accept: How to Decide What Privacy Risks to Inherit

This microcredential provides a comprehensive introduction to the essential tools and techniques required for modern computational data analysis. The program combines classroom and self-study learning to build foundational skills in Linux, Python, version control with Git, cybersecurity, and high performance computing (HPC).
Participants gain hands-on experience with essential computational tools and methods and develop practical skills.
Whether you are beginning to integrate computational tools into your workflow or seek to expand your knowledge, this microcredential offers a structured pathway to becoming proficient in key areas of data analytics.
Teaching classes run from October 20 to November 10, 2026. An additional three optional classes are scheduled on November 12, 17, and 19 to provide help with final projects.
The deadline to apply for this microcredential is September 25, 2026.
title: Microcredential in Practical Foundations for Data Analytics (7 parts)
